title: "Bayesian Optimization"
description: "A method for optimizing an expensive-to-evaluate objective using a probabilistic model."
term: "Bayesian Optimization"
letter: "B"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Advanced"

## Simple explanation

Bayesian optimization helps find a good setting when testing each candidate
is slow or expensive. It uses results from earlier trials to choose
promising settings to try next.

## Technical explanation

The method builds a probabilistic surrogate model of an objective function
and uses an acquisition function to select the next evaluation. The
surrogate estimates both likely performance and uncertainty. Common
surrogates include Gaussian processes and tree-based models; common
acquisition functions include expected improvement and upper confidence
bound.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Training a model or running a simulation for one hyperparameter setting can
consume substantial time or compute. Bayesian optimization can allocate a
limited trial budget more efficiently than uninformed search, although
performance depends on the search space and optimization setup.

## How it works

1. Evaluate the objective at an initial set of candidates.
2. Fit or update a probabilistic surrogate using the observed results.
3. Use an acquisition function to select a candidate balancing expected
   improvement and uncertainty.
4. Evaluate that candidate and repeat until the budget or stopping
   condition is reached.

## Practical example

A team tuning a model's learning rate and regularization strength can use
validation performance as the objective. Each completed training run
updates the surrogate, which suggests the next pair of settings.

## Common misconceptions

- Bayesian optimization does not guarantee the global optimum.
- The surrogate is an approximation and can be misleading with a poor
  search space or noisy observations.
- It is not always preferable to random search, especially for cheap
  objectives or very high-dimensional spaces.
